Notes: Earliest documented presence: 12th-century author Samau'al b. Yahya al-Maghribi names Tabriz (with Salmas and Khoi) as a place where followers of the pseudo-messiah David Alroy adhered to his movement. Year = midpoint of 12th century (source gives only the century).
After Hulagu Khan founded his dynasty (source gives 1285) many Jews migrated to Tabriz; previously a small Jewish population lived there.
Jewish physician Sa'd al-Dawla, vizier of the Ilkhan Arghun in Tabriz, assassinated 1291. Community of Karaites and Rabbanites attested by Hebrew manuscripts.
After Arghun's death in 1291 Sa'd al-Dawla was murdered and Tabrizi Jews suffered a period of violent persecution instigated by the ulama.
Ghazan's conversion to Islam in 1295 turned conditions for the worse for the Jewish community in Tabriz (relegated again to dhimmi status).
Vizier/historian Rashid al-Din (of Jewish origin) executed 1318; his head was carried around Tabriz as 'the head of the Jew'.
Karaite physician Nafis b. Daud at-Tabrizi moved from Tabriz to Cairo in 1354.

About 100 years after 1318 Miran Shah destroyed Rashid al-Din's tomb and his remains were reburied at the Jewish cemetery (implies an existing Jewish cemetery in Tabriz). Year approximate per source's 'about 100 years later'.

Aq Qoyunlu period (c. 1468-1501; year = approximate midpoint): according to Venetian merchants' reports Jews did not reside permanently in Tabriz and came only for trade. Conflicts with other sources on continuous community.
A Jewish community in Tabriz is documented in the 16th century. Year = midpoint of century.
16th century: Yemenite traveler Zechariah al-Dhahiri visited Tabriz and described deteriorating conditions of Jewish life there (Sefer ha-Musar). Year = midpoint of century.
Persecutions under Safavid rulers Abbas I and Abbas II severely affected the Jews of Tabriz (year = 17th-century midpoint; source gives reigns only); community survived.
Between 1711 and 1713 R. Judah b. Amram Diwan, emissary from Hebron, included Tabriz among his visits to Jewish communities in Persia.
Communities still existed in Tabriz (and Maragheh) in the 18th century; they disappear in the first half of the 19th century. Year = midpoint of century.
Between 1790 and 1797 Jews in Tabriz were accused of a blood libel and massacred.
When David d'Beth Hillel visited Persia in 1828 the Jewish community in Tabriz had already ceased to exist.

In 1830 the Jews of Tabriz were massacred; European travellers later reported Jews of Tabriz continued to practise Judaism in secret. (Dating conflicts with the 1790-97 massacre / 1828 extinction in EJ.)

Before the 1979 revolution Khuzistan, Kashan, Tabriz, Hamedan and Sanandaj together had a small Aramaic-speaking Jewish community of about 4000 people - multi-city aggregate, not Tabriz alone. Year = 1978 (pre-revolution).

Religious-minority count: 5 Jews (kalimi) reside in the city. Census year not stated; cited underlying source (Iranian Sociological Association city profile) was accessed Jan 2008, so year uses that date.
